channel.title: Medical Xpress - latest medical and health news stories
channel.description: Medical Xpress internet news portal provides the latest news on science including: Physics, Nanotechnology, Life Sciences, Space Science, Earth Science, Environment, Health and Medicine.

item.title: Bariatric surgery is effective rescue strategy after GLP-1 receptor agonist failure
item.description: Bariatric surgery is associated with clinically meaningful two-year weight loss after semaglutide or tirzepatide intolerance or inadequate response, according to a study published online Nov. 3 in the Annals of Surgery.

item.title: South African trial tests off-the-shelf killer cells against lymphoma
item.description: South African researchers are testing "off-the-shelf" immune cells against lymphoma that has returned or resisted treatment, investigating an approach that avoids having to manufacture a separate treatment from each patient's own cells.

item.title: Is shorter daylight dragging down your mood? What to know about seasonal affective disorder
item.description: Ever heard of the winter blues? The phrase describes that blah, low-energy feeling that can settle in as days grow shorter, colder and grayer this time of year.

item.title: AI better assesses heart function from MRI than clinicians
item.description: Using artificial intelligence (AI) to assess heart function from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans more strongly predicts survival than interpretation by clinicians, according to a study published online Nov. 2 in The Lancet Digital Health.

item.title: Platform finds hidden flaws in athletes' form
item.description: For the first two laps, the student-athlete on the Syracuse University cross country team ran with flawless form. Then, down the stretch, their times began to slip as fatigue set in.

item.title: Two compounds target drug-resistant brain cancer cells in laboratory tests
item.description: Cancer remains among the most deadly diseases worldwide. Globally, more than 300,000 new cases of brain cancer are reported each year, with glioblastoma, an aggressive form of brain cancer, accounting for over 250,000 deaths. The current standard of care involves the use of temozolomide (TMZ), a chemotherapy medication. However, the tumor can be difficult to control because cancer cells evolve to evade the effects of such treatments. Thus, finding new ways to target these cells is an important area in cancer research.

item.title: Mindfulness therapy assisted by ketamine may strengthen body awareness to reduce opioid cravings
item.description: Researchers from the University of California San Diego School of Medicine have found that adding ketamine to a mindfulness-based treatment for opioid use disorder may strengthen people's ability to recognize and respond to signals from their bodies—changes that may help reduce opioid cravings. The study, published on Nov. 5, 2026, in the Journal of Psychopharmacology, provides new insight into how ketamine-assisted psychotherapy may enhance addiction treatment.

item.title: New research identifies biological differences in pancreatic cancer
item.description: New research from the University of Cincinnati Cancer Center found biological differences in pancreatic cancer tumors and immune environments, opening the possibility for more personalized treatments for different populations.

item.title: Mother and baby's immune cells linked to aggressive placental inflammation in preterm cases
item.description: In a healthy pregnancy, a finely tuned maternal immune response prevents the mother's body from rejecting the growing fetus. But in some pregnancies, this response goes haywire, leading to a potentially dangerous complication known as chronic placental inflammation. To understand what drives this inflammation, researchers led by Nardhy Gomez-Lopez, Ph.D., a professor of obstetrics and gynecology and of pathology and immunology at WashU Medicine, used spatial and single-cell gene and protein expression profiling to map the immune cell landscape of the placenta in mothers who developed chronic placental inflammation, down to individual cells at the junction connecting the mother and fetus.

item.title: DNA 'switch' uncovers new brake on breast cancer growth
item.description: Adelaide University researchers have found a DNA "switch" that helps the body stop the growth of the most common form of breast cancer, providing new insights that could help with future treatments. Up to 80% of breast cancer cases are classified as estrogen receptor-positive (ER+)—meaning their growth is driven by the hormone estrogen.

item.title: Four ways thinking like a strategist can make you a better padel player
item.description: As an avid tennis player, I never imagined an injury would lead me to discover a new sport. But just a few months ago, forced to take a break from tennis, I picked up a padel racket for the first time. I assumed that years of playing tennis would give me a head start; after all, how different could two racket sports really be? To my surprise, the answer was "very."

item.title: Blood protein panel outperforms leading ALS biomarker in distinguishing patients from healthy individuals
item.description: Researchers at Emory University School of Medicine have identified 10 blood proteins that, when analyzed together, can distinguish people with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) from healthy individuals with nearly 98% balanced accuracy. The findings, published in Nature Communications, could pave the way for a blood test that helps doctors recognize ALS earlier.

item.title: Is natural toothpaste really as good as fluoride? Tooth decay expert on the difference
item.description: Natural, herbal and organic toothpastes are becoming familiar sights on store shelves, often promoted as healthier alternatives to conventional products. Some contain ingredients such as aloe vera, neem or green tea. But before changing toothpaste, there is one important question to consider: does it contain fluoride?

item.title: Real-world interpretations of amyloid PET scans demonstrate strong agreement with those of amyloid PET experts
item.description: In routine clinical practice, local radiologists and nuclear medicine physicians can reliably interpret amyloid PET scans to aid in the diagnosis and management of Alzheimer's disease, showing good agreement with interpretations by amyloid PET specialists. According to a new study published in The Journal of Nuclear Medicine, local interpretations of nearly 1,500 scans showed excellent agreement with expert panel assessments, demonstrating that visual reads performed in community settings are highly reliable.

item.title: I'm an athletic trainer—here's how to know when kids' sports are too intense
item.description: At a recent T-ball game, I was talking with another father who mentioned that his son had never played before. As we watched our children falling over trying to scoop up a ground ball, we laughed about how they were still figuring everything out. There was something refreshing about seeing kids learn a game without worrying about how well they were playing.

item.title: Drug restores kidney cell function in experimental models of rare Lowe syndrome
item.description: Over two decades of research into the cellular mechanisms underlying Lowe syndrome have led to the identification of a potential therapeutic strategy for this rare genetic disorder, which affects the eyes, nervous system and kidneys. The findings are described in a study published in Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy, by the research group led by Antonella De Matteis, coordinator of the Cell Biology Program at the Telethon Institute of Genetics and Medicine (TIGEM) in Pozzuoli and full professor of cell biology at the University of Naples Federico II in the Department of Molecular Medicine and Medical Biotechnology.

item.title: Breast milk fatty acids linked to infant motor development
item.description: A new study has found an association between odd- and branched-chain fatty acid (OBCFA) levels in breast milk and infant motor development, providing new population-based evidence for research on early-life nutrition and neurodevelopment.

item.title: Vitamin K deficiency on the rise as more parents decline recommended shots for their newborns
item.description: The American Academy of Pediatrics has recommended a single intramuscular dose of vitamin K for newborns since 1961; however, in the last decade parents have increasingly elected to skip the shot.

item.title: Crigler-Najjar syndrome: Gene therapy maintains its efficacy four years after treatment
item.description: The New England Journal of Medicine has published a study on the long-term efficacy of AAV8-mediated gene therapy (GNT0003) in patients with Crigler-Najjar syndrome, an extremely rare congenital liver disorder affecting approximately 500 people in Europe. It is caused by a deficiency of UGT1A1, an enzyme required for bilirubin metabolism. The accumulation of this substance can lead to irreversible neurological damage and, in the most severe cases, death.

item.title: This weightlifting technique can help older adults stay fit and independent as they age
item.description: If you're over 60 and have started lifting weights, you've probably been told to take it slowly. Lift steadily, lower steadily, keep it controlled.

item.title: Drug discovery by scientists joins world's largest trial of Parkinson's treatments
item.description: A liver drug could be used to slow down the progression of Parkinson's disease as it joins the world's largest trial of treatments for the condition.

item.title: AI-powered smartwatch detects high blood pressure with sensitivity similar to office screening
item.description: Smartwatches may be able to detect hypertension (high blood pressure) with the help of an artificial intelligence (AI) system that interprets sensor readings, a paper in Nature reports. Tests of the system, trialed using a consumer smartwatch, show that it can detect hypertension at similar sensitivities to traditional office-based blood pressure screening methods.

item.title: New research identifies promising strategy to support eating disorder recovery for adults with autism
item.description: In the first study of its kind, researchers from the University of Aberdeen and the University of Edinburgh worked with adults with autism who had received treatment for eating disorders. Participants viewed personalized, autism-affirming peer support, where people with shared lived experience support one another, as potentially valuable for recovery. The research is published in the journal Eating Disorders.

item.title: Genetic variant may increase the risk of pneumonia
item.description: Pneumonia is a common and sometimes serious infection that affects 20,000–30,000 people in Sweden every year. Well-known risk factors include advanced age, smoking and underlying medical conditions. In a new study published in eBioMedicine, researchers at Lund University and Skåne University Hospital have shown that genetic differences in the innate immune system can also influence the risk of developing the disease.

item.title: Metformin may lower risk of long COVID or death by 53% when prescribed early
item.description: Long COVID—or new-onset symptoms or worsening health conditions after SARS-CoV-2 infection—can lower quality of life. Finding a way to prevent it would be a welcome relief for those worried about the long-term effects of the viral infection.

item.title: Researchers develop more precise way to identify preeclampsia from electronic health records
item.description: Researchers at King's College London have found a more effective method for identifying preeclampsia from electronic health records (EHRs), allowing them to capture cases and associated adverse outcomes that existing methods may miss.

item.title: Updated guidance refines how doctors assess cardiogenic shock and track treatment response
item.description: The Society for Cardiovascular Angiography & Interventions (SCAI) has released the 2026 SCAI SHOCK Classification Expert Consensus Update, providing refined guidance to help clinicians from diverse settings prioritize and recognize inadequate organ perfusion across a broad range of shock presentations, assess shock severity over time, and determine whether treatment is restoring adequate circulation.

item.title: One nap doesn't fit all: How childcare's link to napping flips with age
item.description: A well-napped child is a cheerful and happy child. In a world where both parents have to work, most children spend their first five years attending childcare, right around the time they transition from regular daytime naps to sleeping through the night. A recent study published in Sleep Medicine investigated whether attending childcare changes the number of times a child naps on that day compared with days spent at home, and how that relationship shifts as children grow older.

item.title: Manosphere, tobacco and gambling are driving avoidable harm and premature deaths among men, studies find
item.description: Men are suffering poor health and dying younger while the companies that profit from their misery are turning over billions of dollars.

item.title: Obesity drugs could lead to new ways to protect the brain
item.description: Drugs such as semaglutide and tirzepatide are already used to treat obesity and type 2 diabetes, but they also influence biological processes important for brain function. In a new review published in Science, researchers at the University of Gothenburg and the University of Copenhagen assessed the available evidence.
